quests.instruction: Count the links from the start: find the second one
quests.textToSpeak: in my last role I managed a team of six
quests.hint: Count the links from the start and stop at two.
quests.explanation: The -ed of 'managed' ends in /d/, and it lands on the weak /ə/ of 'a', so 'managed a team' is one chunk. 'Role I' comes first through /l/, and 'team of' follows.
quests.flowRule: Thought groups: Fluent speakers connect words across a whole phrase, so one sentence can contain several links. The instruction tells you which one to find; listen to the sounds on each side of a boundary.

quests.instruction: Find the link carried by a 'th' sound
quests.textToSpeak: what attracted me is the chance to grow with other talented people
quests.hint: Say the candidates slowly and listen for a soft, breathy end sliding into a vowel.
quests.explanation: The /ð/ of 'with' is released into the weak /ʌ/ of 'other'. 'Attracted me' and 'chance to' do not link, so this is the one place where a consonant meets a vowel before 'talented'. Interviewers hear this phrase constantly.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/θ/ and /ð/): The 'th' sounds at the end of a word stay in the airflow and connect to a following vowel instead of stopping.

quests.instruction: Which link is carried by a sound you can hold?
quests.textToSpeak: my main weakness is that I sometimes take on too much
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in a held sound, followed by a word that starts with a vowel.
quests.explanation: The /s/ of 'weakness' flows into the /ɪ/ of 'is', so a candidate's honest answer keeps its pace. 'Take on' and 'that I' link through stops, so they are different in kind.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (continuous sounds): Sounds you can hold, such as /s/, /z/, /f/, /v/ and /ʃ/, glide directly into a following vowel without restarting.

quests.instruction: Which pair would sound broken if you paused between the words?
quests.textToSpeak: I'd like to start by thanking everyone for being here today
quests.hint: Only one pair in this sentence joins smoothly. Look for an -ing word.
quests.explanation: A pause there turns a warm thank-you into a recited line. The /ŋ/ of 'thanking' runs on into the /e/ of 'everyone', so the pair behaves like one word.
quests.flowRule: Smooth versus separated speech: Fluent speakers keep a phrase in one flow and pause only between thought groups. A gap inside a linked pair sounds choppy even when every word is clear, so train your ear to hear the join rather than the separate words.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a word ending in two consonants joins a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: sales have increased in every region since last year
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in something like /st/, /nd/, /lt/ or /nz/ before a vowel.
quests.explanation: The -ed of 'increased' is a /t/ after /s/, and it lands on the vowel of 'in', so the past participle stays audible. 'Have increased' and 'in every' link through single consonants.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by a nasal sound?
quests.textToSpeak: questions can wait until later but please interrupt if anything is unclear
quests.hint: A hum connects better than a stop does. Where is the hum?
quests.explanation: A presenter inviting interruptions speaks easily, so the links run on: the /ŋ/ of 'anything' hums into the /ɪ/ of 'is'. 'Wait until', 'interrupt if' and 'if anything' link through other sounds.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (nasals): A word ending in /m/ or /n/ keeps your voice running, so the nasal sound flows directly into a following vowel with no gap.

quests.instruction: Which word-final r connects to the next vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: we can offer a discount if you commit to a longer contract
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in -er before a weak vowel.
quests.explanation: A salesperson would say this in one relaxed breath. The written r of 'offer' appears before the weak /ə/ of 'a' (always, in rhotic accents), and 'discount if' links through /t/.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which two words belong together in this idiom?
quests.textToSpeak: I think we can work something out
quests.hint: Only one pair in this sentence joins a consonant to a vowel. Look for an -ing sound.
quests.explanation: 'Work something out' is an idiom and stays together. The /ŋ/ of 'something' runs into the vowel of 'out', and since it is the only link, it is the one the listener hears as the point of the sentence.
quests.flowRule: Smooth versus separated speech: Fluent speakers keep a phrase in one flow and pause only between thought groups. A gap inside a linked pair sounds choppy even when every word is clear, so train your ear to hear the join rather than the separate words.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an /l/?
quests.textToSpeak: we could settle on a price around four hundred
quests.hint: Your tongue tip stays up for /l/. Which word ends that way before a vowel?
quests.explanation: The syllabic /l/ of 'settle' runs into the vowel of 'on'. 'On a' and 'price around' link through /n/ and /s/. Price talk is said quickly and confidently.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (/l/): A word-final /l/ stays voiced and slides into the vowel of the next word, so the two words sound like one continuous stretch.

quests.instruction: Which pair merges into a new sound in casual speech?
quests.textToSpeak: I completely understand your frustration and I'd like to put this right
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ followed by a word that starts with a 'y' sound.
quests.explanation: 'Understand your' becomes 'understandjer' as /d/ and /j/ blend into /dʒ/. In a customer-service reply this is common, though some agents keep the sounds apart to sound formal.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Find the link that keeps a past-tense -ed audible
quests.textToSpeak: I've added a note so you won't have to explain it twice
quests.hint: Listen for the small /t/ or /d/ at the end of a past verb, joined to the next vowel.
quests.explanation: The /d/ of 'added' (/ɪd/) lands on the weak /ə/ of 'a', so the agent's report sounds smooth. 'Explain it' and others link through other sounds, but only 'added a' carries a past tense.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a written r returns before a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: is there anything I can help you with today
quests.hint: Look for a word spelled with 're' before a vowel.
quests.explanation: In non-rhotic accents the /r/ at the end of 'there' appears before 'anything' but not in 'there now'; in rhotic accents it is always present. 'Anything I' links through /ŋ/ in the same sentence.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a linking /r/?
quests.textToSpeak: I'd prefer a seat near the exit if possible
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in -er before 'an'.
quests.explanation: 'Prefer' ends in a written r, so the /r/ appears before the weak /ə/ of 'a'. 'The exit' and 'exit if' have their own links, but only 'prefer a' carries a linking r.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Find the link that slides through a 'y' sound
quests.textToSpeak: please be at the gate at least thirty minutes before departure
quests.hint: A glide like 'y' is quiet. Listen very closely at the vowel-to-vowel boundary.
quests.explanation: Airport instructions are said clearly, but the glide is still there: the /iː/ at the end of 'be' leads into the vowel of 'at' with a light /j/. 'At least' joins no vowels, because 'least' begins with /l/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a consonant cluster?
quests.textToSpeak: my bag hasn't arrived but the staff have no information
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in two consonants before a vowel.
quests.explanation: Travellers complaining at a desk speak fast, so the cluster is light, but the /n/ and /t/ of 'hasn't' still carry into the weak /ə/ of 'arrived'. 'No information' joins two vowels with a faint /w/, a different kind of link.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.

quests.instruction: Which word-final r connects to the next vowel?
quests.textToSpeak: we got lost on the way there and ended up miles away
quests.hint: Say the candidates slowly: an /r/ shows up at one boundary only.
quests.explanation: Telling a story is done in long runs, so the links carry the narrative. 'There' ends in a final /r/ that links into the weak /ən/ of 'and', and the chain continues through 'and ended', 'ended up' and 'miles away'.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Where does a faint 'y' appear between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: she looked at me as if I'd lost my mind
quests.hint: Two vowel sounds touch with no consonant between. After a high, smiling vowel, listen for a faint 'y'.
quests.explanation: Storytelling speeds up at moments like this. The /iː/ of 'me' leads into the vowel of 'as' with a light /j/, while 'looked at', 'as if' and 'if I'd' are consonant-to-vowel links.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Spot the vowel-to-vowel link that takes a 'y' glide
quests.textToSpeak: it turned out everyone had already left by the time we arrived
quests.hint: Say each candidate slowly. A light /j/ appears between two vowels only once.
quests.explanation: The end of a story is said fast and low. 'We' ends in /iː/ and 'arrived' begins with the weak /ə/, so a light /j/ slips between them. 'Turned out', 'out everyone' and 'had already' are consonant-to-vowel links.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a written r returns before a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: hello this is Sam from the clinic calling to confirm your appointment
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in 'our' before a vowel.
quests.explanation: A voicemail script is read smoothly. 'Your' ends in a written r, so the /r/ appears before the weak /ə/ of 'appointment' in most accents. 'Confirm your' does not link, because /m/ meets /j/.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Which link is released from a stop (p, t, k, b, d or g)?
quests.textToSpeak: call me back when you get a chance or leave a message
quests.hint: Pause after each word and notice which pause feels forced: that is where a stop link sits.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'get' lands on the weak /ə/ of 'a', so 'get a chance' sounds like one word. 'Chance or' and 'leave a' link through /s/ and /v/, which can be held. Voicemail messages are said quickly.
quests.flowRule: Consonant-to-Vowel Linking (stops): When a word ends in a stop consonant (/p/, /t/, /k/, /b/, /d/, /g/) and the next word starts with a vowel sound, the stop is released straight into that vowel with no pause between the words.

quests.instruction: Which link has a light /j/ ('y') glide between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: we're out of the office till Tuesday but we check messages daily
quests.hint: Look for a vowel sound ending a word and another starting the next. One of them ends like 'ee' or 'eye'.
quests.explanation: Before a vowel 'the' is /ðiː/, ending high and forward, so a light /j/ slips into 'office'. 'Out of' links through /t/. 'Office till' does not link, because /s/ meets /t/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which pair is joined by an -ed ending?
quests.textToSpeak: overall you've exceeded expectations and I'd like to thank you formally
quests.hint: The past-tense ending matters for meaning. Which boundary carries it?
quests.explanation: Praise sounds fluent when the -ed lands where it should: the /d/ of 'exceeded' (/ɪd/) runs into the vowel of 'expectations'. 'Expectations and' and 'and I'd' link through other sounds, so the sentence is a chain.
quests.flowRule: Past-tense endings link too: A final -ed (/t/ or /d/) joins a following vowel, which also keeps the past-tense signal audible.

quests.instruction: Which link carries a linking /r/?
quests.textToSpeak: the area where I'd like to see better planning
quests.hint: Look for a word ending in 're' before a vowel.
quests.explanation: Managers giving feedback say this at a measured pace. The final /r/ of 'where' links into the /aɪ/ of 'I'd', while 'the area' is a vowel-to-vowel link with a faint /j/, which is a different kind.
quests.flowRule: Linking /r/ (accent-dependent): In rhotic accents (most of North America, Scotland, Ireland) a word-final r is always pronounced, so it simply connects to a following vowel. In non-rhotic accents (for example most of England, Australia, New Zealand) the r is silent before a consonant or a pause but usually returns before a vowel, as in 'far away'. Either way, the two words connect.

quests.instruction: Where does a faint 'w' appear between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: can you show us the latest numbers
quests.hint: The first vowel of the link finishes with the lips rounded. Which pair?
quests.explanation: A manager asking this wants a quick, friendly tone. After the /əʊ/ of 'show', a faint /w/ eases into the weak vowel of 'us'. 'Latest numbers' does not link.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Where do two sounds blend into one in fast, informal speech?
quests.textToSpeak: so what brings you here today
quests.hint: Two sounds fuse into one at a word boundary. Listen for a 'ch', 'j', 'sh' or 'zh' where you would expect two separate sounds.
quests.explanation: 'Brings you' sounds like 'bringzhu', with /z/ and /j/ blending into /ʒ/. It is an easy, friendly question at a networking event, and the merge makes it sound relaxed.
quests.flowRule: Yod-coalescence (informal speech): When a word ending in /t/, /d/, /s/ or /z/ is followed by 'you' or 'your', the two sounds often merge into one: /t/+/j/ becomes /tʃ/ ('got you' sounds like 'gotcha'), /d/+/j/ becomes /dʒ/ ('did you' like 'didja'), /s/+/j/ becomes /ʃ/ and /z/+/j/ becomes /ʒ/. This is a normal informal reduction, not a mistake, and careful speakers may keep the sounds apart.

quests.instruction: Find the link that slides through a 'y' sound
quests.textToSpeak: I'm actually in town for a few days visiting a friend
quests.hint: No consonant is released here. The tongue just glides from one vowel to the next.
quests.explanation: Small talk is casual, so glides are quick: the /i/ at the end of 'actually' slips into the /ɪ/ of 'in' with a light /j/. 'For a' and 'visiting a' link through a written r and /ŋ/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Which pair belongs together in this farewell?
quests.textToSpeak: I hope we meet again soon
quests.hint: Only one pair in this sentence joins smoothly.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of 'meet' lands on the weak /ə/ of 'again', so the farewell sounds like one phrase. A pause there makes a warm wish sound stiff.
quests.flowRule: Smooth versus separated speech: Fluent speakers keep a phrase in one flow and pause only between thought groups. A gap inside a linked pair sounds choppy even when every word is clear, so train your ear to hear the join rather than the separate words.

quests.instruction: Where does a faint 'y' appear between two vowels?
quests.textToSpeak: hopefully we'll hear from them by Friday afternoon
quests.hint: Which pair has a vowel on both sides and a high front vowel on the left?
quests.explanation: Day-and-time phrases are said as one unit, so the glide is almost always there. The /eɪ/ of 'Friday' leads into the vowel of 'afternoon' with a light /j/.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /j/ glide: After vowels made with the tongue high and forward (/iː/, /eɪ/, /aɪ/, /ɔɪ/), many speakers slide through a light /j/ ('y') before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Spot the vowel-to-vowel link that takes a 'w' glide
quests.textToSpeak: he's one of those people who always asks for more
quests.hint: A glide like 'w' is quiet. Listen very closely at the vowel-to-vowel boundary.
quests.explanation: A speaker describing a personality says this fluently: 'who' ends in /uː/ and 'always' begins with /ɔː/, so a faint /w/ slides in. 'One of' and 'always asks' link through consonants.
quests.flowRule: Vowel-to-Vowel Linking with a /w/ glide: After vowels made with rounded lips (/uː/, /əʊ/, /aʊ/), many speakers slide through a light /w/ before the next vowel. It is a natural transition, not a written letter, and it is subtle.

quests.instruction: Find the link where a word ending in two consonants joins a vowel
quests.textToSpeak: it's best if we sort this out as soon as possible
quests.hint: Skip the single consonants. Which ending has two or more?
quests.explanation: Polite proposals are said in one flowing line. The /st/ of 'best' is often light, but the /s/ still runs into the vowel of 'if'. 'Out as' and 'soon as' link through single consonants.
quests.flowRule: Linking after consonant clusters: When a word ends in two or three consonants, the last one still connects into a following vowel, so the ending is carried across the boundary smoothly.
